summary: Extends LSP ping to find faults in point-to-multipoint MPLS label switched paths. It does not replace existing LSP ping mechanisms but clarifies how they apply to the point-to-multipoint case. It updates RFC 4379.

eli5.summary: Instead of one road from A to B, some paths branch out like a tree. This explains how to send a test signal along such a tree and find where a branch is broken.

subtitle: How to ping and trace MPLS paths that branch to many receivers, without flooding the sender with replies.

tldr.problem: LSP ping could test point-to-point MPLS paths, but a point-to-multipoint path replicates packets to many egresses, so testing it raises new questions about identifying the path and handling many replies.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds new sub-TLVs to name a P2MP LSP, a P2MP Responder Identifier TLV to limit who answers, an Echo Jitter TLV to spread replies out, and a Respond Only If TTL Expired flag for traceroute.
tldr.outcome: It extends and updates RFC 4379 rather than replacing it, and it is a Proposed Standard that no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating.

facts.label: Global Flags
facts.value: V flag at bit 15, T flag at bit 14

today: RFC 6425 is a Proposed Standard from November 2011 that updates RFC 4379. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Extending LSP Ping to Branching Paths
sections.content:
RFC 4379 describes LSP ping: MPLS echo request and echo reply messages that check that the data plane of a point-to-point (P2P) Label Switched Path works and matches the control plane. This RFC applies the same techniques to point-to-multipoint (P2MP) LSPs, for which requirements are in RFC 4461 and RSVP-TE signaling is in RFC 4875, with multicast LDP in RFC 6388.

The design rule is to reuse or extend existing mechanisms rather than invent new ones. As with P2P, echo requests must follow the same data path as normal MPLS packets, which here means they are replicated to every egress (leaf) of the tree. Checking the liveness of the control plane is not part of LSP ping. To avoid denial-of-service attacks, the RFC recommends a rate limiter on incoming LSP ping traffic.
sections.eli5: The old test message went along one road. Now the road splits like a tree, so the test message gets copied at every split and runs to every end.

sections.title: Why P2MP LSPs Need Their Own Handling
sections.content:
LSP ping is modeled on ping and traceroute. Ping mode (connectivity verification) checks that a packet reaches an egress that really is an egress for the path. Traceroute mode (fault isolation) sends the packet to the control plane of each transit router to check that forwarding matches what the routing protocols decided. A suggested pattern is to ping periodically and run a traceroute only if the ping fails.

For P2MP LSPs, the test is that packets entering at the ingress end up at the intended egresses. The echo request is forwarded like any other packet on the LSP, so it is replicated at branch points. Each egress sends an echo reply to the ingress.

A large tree can have many egresses, and their replies could arrive at about the same time and cause congestion at or near the ingress. The RFC gives two controls: responders can randomly delay (jitter) their replies, and the initiator can limit a request to one specific egress.
sections.eli5: If a hundred houses all reply to one test message at the same moment, the mailbox at the start overflows. So the houses are asked to wait a random moment, or only one house is asked to answer.

sections.title: Naming the P2MP LSP Under Test
sections.content:
The echo request keeps the basic LSP ping packet structure. To say which P2MP LSP is tested, it MUST carry a Target FEC Stack TLV with exactly one of four new sub-TLVs.

For a P2MP MPLS TE LSP, this is an RSVP P2MP IPv4 Session (sub-type 17, length 20) or RSVP P2MP IPv6 Session (sub-type 18, length 56) sub-TLV. They carry fields from the RSVP-TE P2MP SESSION and SENDER_TEMPLATE objects: P2MP ID, Tunnel ID, Extended Tunnel ID, Tunnel Sender Address and LSP ID.

For a multicast LDP LSP, it is a Multicast P2MP LDP FEC Stack (sub-type 19) or Multicast MP2MP LDP FEC Stack (sub-type 20) sub-TLV. Both hold an Address Family, an Address Length, the Root LSR Address and an Opaque Value that identifies the LSP in the context of the root. The Address Length MUST be 4 for IPv4 and 16 for IPv6.

For multipoint-to-multipoint LSPs, any leaf can be treated as the head of a P2MP tree for OAM purposes.
sections.eli5: Before testing a tree of roads, you must say which tree you mean. These new labels are like the tree's name tag.

sections.title: Controlling Replies: Responder ID, Jitter and the T Flag
sections.content:
The P2MP Responder Identifier TLV (type 11) appears only in echo requests and limits who replies. It holds sub-TLVs: Egress Address (sub-types 1 for IPv4 and 2 for IPv6) and Node Address (sub-types 3 for IPv4 and 4 for IPv6). With a Node Address, a node MUST reply only if the address is one of its own. With an Egress Address, a node MUST reply only if it lies on the path to that address. The Egress Address form needs upstream nodes to know the leaf, which RSVP-TE provides but multicast LDP does not, so it SHOULD NOT be used with a multicast LDP FEC.

The Echo Jitter TLV (type 12, length 4) carries a Jitter Time in milliseconds. A responder MUST wait a random time between zero and that value before replying.

The T flag (Respond Only If TTL Expired) is a new bit in the Global Flags field. If it is 0, the node processes the request. If it is 1 and the MPLS TTL is 1, the node processes it. If it is 1 and the TTL is more than 1, the node MUST drop the request without replying.

Finally, the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV from RFC 6424 MUST be supported for P2MP, and the older Downstream Mapping TLV MUST NOT be included in an echo request.
sections.eli5: You can say "only the house at this address, please answer", or "everyone wait a random moment before answering". There is also a rule: "answer only if my message ran out of steps at your door."

sections.title: How Initiators and Responders Behave
sections.content:
The initiator follows RFC 4379 and puts one of the new FEC sub-TLVs in the Target FEC Stack TLV. Echo requests go through the data plane and cannot be stopped from reaching all egresses, so limiting replies is done with the Responder Identifier TLV. Leaving it out means all egresses should reply. Jitter SHOULD be used for P2MP LSPs, though it MAY be omitted for simple LSPs or when Node Address sub-TLVs are used. If no Echo Jitter TLV is present, an egress SHOULD NOT add extra delay.

LSP ping MUST NOT be used to measure round-trip time, because P2MP LSPs are unidirectional and replies often return through the control plane. A responder MUST set the Timestamp Received fields before applying any jitter delay.

A responder first rate-limits, then checks the packet, then asks its control plane whether it is part of the LSP. If not, it replies by RFC 4379 rules. If it is, the Responder Identifier TLV decides whether the request is aimed at it.

Return codes vary by role. Transit and branch nodes MAY return code 8 (label switched at stack-depth). Egress nodes MAY return code 3 (replying router is an egress). A transit node that is on the LSP but not on the path to the tested egress SHOULD NOT reply unless there is an error to report.
sections.eli5: Each router checks whether it is on the tree, and whether the message is meant for it. If it is, it answers according to its job: passing along, or at the end.

sections.title: Bud Nodes and Traceroute
sections.content:
A bud node is both an egress and a transit or branch node, so its behavior depends on the Responder Identifier TLV. With no such TLV it acts as egress plus branch. With a Node Address it acts as egress plus branch if the address matches, otherwise it sends no reply. With an Egress Address it acts as an egress only if the address matches, as a transit node if it lies on the path to the address, and sends nothing otherwise.

Traceroute sends requests with sequentially increasing TTL values. A valid reply from one egress does not end a P2MP traceroute, so the RFC RECOMMENDS a configurable upper limit on the TTL. Because bud and egress nodes keep replying to deeper probes, the T flag is RECOMMENDED for P2MP traceroute only. It does not help when penultimate hop popping is used, since those nodes get no label.

If no reply comes, the initiator SHOULD still send the next request with a larger TTL, although it MAY stop. When the request is aimed at more than one node, the Downstream IP Address in the Downstream Detailed Mapping TLV MUST be the ALLROUTERS multicast address. A cross-over node reports only the outgoing interface for each input interface.
sections.eli5: Some routers are both an end of a branch and a stop on the way to more branches. They have to work out which role the question is for. In a step-by-step trace, you stop at a sensible depth because the tree has no single end.

sections.title: Non-Compliant Routers and Operations
sections.content:
If a node on a P2MP LSP does not support LSP ping, it sends no reply and the initiator may get a wrong result. There is no protection against this. A non-compliant egress still lets traceroute verify the path nearly all the way. A non-compliant branch or transit node should not affect ping mode but will not respond in traceroute mode.

For operations, the RFC advises cautious use. Pinging all egresses can cause congestion near the ingress, and careless timers, especially for traceroute, can degrade the network. Management interfaces should let an operator limit a request to a single egress and disable all active LSP ping operations. A MIB module is needed, which should be a simple extension of the P2P LSP ping MIB module.
sections.eli5: If one router in the tree does not know the game, it stays silent and the test result can look wrong. Be gentle with how often you test, so the test itself does not cause traffic jams.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no security concerns beyond those of RFC 4379. Because P2MP LSPs can have many egresses, there is a stronger need to rate-limit LSP ping traffic reaching the control plane on the LSP ping well-known UDP port. That rate limiting might give false indications of LSP failure.

IANA registered the new sub-TLV types 17 to 20 and TLV types 11 and 12, and created a Global Flags registry with the V flag at bit 15 and the T flag at bit 14.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is dangerous here, but because so many replies are possible, routers must limit how many test messages they accept. That can sometimes make a healthy path look broken.
